title: Parrots May Call Each Other by Name
hook: Parrots might do more than mimic. An analysis of pet-parrot recordings suggests they use specific 'names' for particular people and animals — even ones not in the room.
key_points: Researchers analyzed hundreds of recordings of pet parrots' everyday vocalizations.
Many birds appeared to use specific names to identify particular people, animals, or companions.
Some referred to an individual who wasn't present — a hint of meaning, not just imitation.
A few used names creatively, like saying their own name to grab attention.
If it holds up, parrot 'talk' may carry referential meaning, not just copied sounds.
content_html: We tend to dismiss a talking parrot as a clever copycat — repeating words with no idea what they mean. A new study, reported by ScienceDaily, suggests that may sell parrots short. Analyzing hundreds of recordings of pet parrots, researchers found signs that many birds use specific "names" to pick out particular people, animals, and companions.
extra_html: The telling detail is that some parrots seemed to refer to an individual who wasn't even in the room — the kind of thing that's hard to explain as pure imitation, because there was no sound to copy in the moment. Others used names inventively, such as saying their own name to get attention. If the pattern holds up under closer study, it would point to parrot vocalizations carrying referential meaning — sounds that stand for specific things — rather than being empty mimicry. It's early evidence, and the researchers are careful not to overclaim, but it adds parrots to a growing list of animals whose communication looks richer the more closely we listen.

flashcards.prompt: What did the parrot-recording study suggest beyond simple mimicry?
flashcards.back_html: That parrots may use specific names to refer to particular individuals — people, animals, or companions — sometimes even ones that aren't present.

flashcards.prompt: Which observation hints that parrots use names with meaning, not just imitation?

choices.text: Some parrots referred to an individual who wasn't in the room
The parrots repeated every word a human said
The parrots only made sounds when being fed

flashcards.explanation_html: Referring to someone who isn't present suggests the name stands for that individual in the bird's mind — a sign of reference, which goes beyond echoing sounds back.

flashcards.prompt: How did the researchers gather their evidence?

choices.text: By analyzing hundreds of recordings of pet parrots
By teaching the parrots an entirely new human language
By scanning the parrots' brains during sleep

flashcards.explanation_html: The study drew on a large set of recordings of pet parrots' natural vocalizations, looking for patterns in how birds used particular sounds for particular individuals.
